transcript:
[doctor] Hi, how are you doing today?

[patient] I've been better, honestly. My throat has been killing me for the past three days.

[doctor] I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been going on?

[patient] Sure. My throat has been incredibly sore for the last three days, and it's not getting any better. It's constant and makes it hard to sleep or eat anything that's not soft.

[doctor] I see. Have you noticed any other symptoms along with the sore throat?

[patient] Yes, I've had some pretty bad headaches on and off, and I feel really tired all the time. I haven't had a fever, though.

[doctor] Alright, so you've been dealing with headaches and fatigue as well. Have you lost your voice or had trouble swallowing?

[patient] Yes, I've lost my voice quite a bit, and swallowing is really painful.

[doctor] That sounds tough. Can you tell me more about how the sore throat is affecting your sleep?

[patient] The pain wakes me up at night, so I'm not sleeping well at all. It's really frustrating.

[doctor] I can imagine. What kind of work do you do?

[patient] I'm a high school teacher.

[doctor] Okay. Have you noticed if any of your students or colleagues have been sick recently?

[patient] Not really, but you know how schools are. There's always something going around.

[doctor] Absolutely. Now, let's talk about your general health. Have you had any episodes like this before?

[patient] Not really. I get the occasional sore throat, but nothing this severe.

[doctor] Understood. Do you have any other medical conditions or take any regular medications?

[patient] No, I'm generally pretty healthy. I don't take any regular medications.

[doctor] Okay. Let’s review your vitals and do a physical exam. Your blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, heart rate is 80 bpm, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 98.6°F, and your oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.

[patient] Alright.

[doctor] On examination, your throat looks quite red but there's no pus or exudate. You do have some tender lymph nodes in your neck, though. Your lungs are clear, and your heart sounds are normal. Neurologically, there are no focal deficits.

[patient] What does all that mean?

[doctor] It means your throat is inflamed, which is why it's so painful. The tender lymph nodes indicate your body is fighting something off, but your lungs and heart are in good shape, and there's no sign of a more serious neurological issue.

[patient] Okay, that's a relief.

[doctor] We did a rapid strep test, and it came back negative. We're still waiting on the throat culture results to see if there’s any bacterial infection. I’ve also ordered a complete blood count with differential to check for underlying bacterial infection. Those results are pending.

[patient] So, what should I do in the meantime?

[doctor] For now, I’m prescribing Hydrocodone-Acetaminophen 5-325 mg. Take one tablet every 6 hours as needed for severe pain, but no more than 15 tablets. Drink plenty of fluids, get as much rest as you can, and use throat lozenges to help soothe the pain.

[patient] Got it. Anything else?

[doctor] Yes, I also recommend avoiding tobacco and reducing alcohol consumption as it can irritate your throat further. Stick to a nutritious diet that’s easy to swallow—soft foods are best.

[patient] Okay, I can do that.

[doctor] I want you to come back in a week for a follow-up. We’ll reassess your symptoms and review the throat culture and blood test results. If there’s no improvement, I’ll refer you to an infectious disease specialist, Dr. James Anderson.

[patient] Will do. Thanks, Doc.

[doctor] Before you go, do you have any questions about the plan?

[patient] Not really, except, why an infectious disease specialist?

[doctor] If your symptoms persist, it could mean there's an underlying infection that needs a specialist's attention. Dr. Anderson can provide you with more targeted care if necessary.

[patient] I understand. Thanks for explaining.

[doctor] No problem. And remember, if things get worse or you have any new concerns, don’t hesitate to come back sooner.

[patient] Will do. Thanks again.

[doctor] You’re welcome. Take care and see you in a week.
